find: his hair was neither crisply curled nor smooth, brown of color.
replace: his hair was neither crisply curled nor smooth. He was brown of complexion.
reason: أَسْمَرَ اللَّوْنِ describes his complexion, not his hair. It is accusative like رَبْعَةً and حَسَنَ الْجِسْمِ, and the same hadith with the same isnad in Jāmi‘ al-Tirmidhī places أسمر اللون before the hair clause (dataset English there: “brown in complexion”).
The isnad reads عَنْ أَبِي إِسْحَاقَ (Abū Isḥāq), not Ibn Isḥāq.

find: was neither curly nor lank-haired, of medium height
reason: The Arabic has no hair-texture phrase (no جعد / سبط); it goes straight from رَجُلا مَرْبُوعًا to بَعِيدَ مَا بَيْنَ الْمَنْكِبَيْنِ. The English may follow a different manuscript, so a scholar should confirm before removing it. Separately, the Arabic has an odd الْيُسْرَى (“the left”) after أُذُنَيْهِ.

find: My maternal aunt Hind asked the son of Abu Hala
replace: I asked my maternal uncle Hind, the son of Abu Hala
reason: سَأَلْتُ خَالِي هِنْدَ بْنَ أَبِي هَالَةَ: al-Ḥasan is the one asking (سألتُ, “I asked”), and خالي is “my maternal uncle”. Hind ibn Abī Hāla is a man, Khadīja’s son and so al-Ḥasan’s uncle.

find: someone who did not reflect on him would consider him haughty
replace: someone who did not look at him carefully would think his nose high-bridged
reason: يَحْسَبُهُ مَنْ لَمْ يَتَأَمَّلْهُ أَشَمَّ comes straight after أَقْنَى الْعِرْنَيْنِ (the nose). أشمّ usually means a high, raised nose bridge in this context; “haughty” takes the figurative sense. Interpretive, so needs a scholar.

find: He replied:" endowed with a lean heel.”
reason: Shu‘ba’s question about ضَلِيعَ الْفَمِ is answered with the explanation of مَنْهُوسَ الْعَقِبِ; the other two answers are missing. The dataset Arabic has no Q&A at all. The parallel in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim has it: مَا ضَلِيعُ الْفَمِ قَالَ عَظِيمُ الْفَمِ … مَا أَشْكَلُ الْعَيْنِ قَالَ طَوِيلُ شَقِّ الْعَيْنِ … مَا مَنْهُوسُ الْعَقِبِ قَالَ قَلِيلُ لَحْمِ الْعَقِبِ. Needs the full Arabic and a translator.

find: The date palms then bore their annual crop,
replace: The date palms then bore fruit that same year,
reason: فَحَمَلَتِ النَّخْلُ مِنْ عَامِهَا: مِنْ عَامِهَا means “in that same year” (date palms normally take years to fruit), which is the point of the report.

find: so it bore its annual crop.
replace: so it bore fruit that same year.
reason: فَحَمَلَتْ مِنْ عَامِهَا: “it bore fruit in that same year”, not “its annual crop”.

find: Umm Hani bint 'Ali ibn Talib said:
replace: Umm Hani bint Abi Talib said:
reason: The isnad reads أُمِّ هَانِئٍ بِنْتِ أَبِي طَالِبٍ. Umm Hāni’ is the daughter of Abū Ṭālib (‘Alī’s sister), not of ‘Alī.

replace: came to Mecca on one occasion
reason: قَدِمَ … مَكَّةَ قَدْمَةً: قَدْمَةً is a noun of single occurrence (“one arrival / once”). Nothing in the Arabic means “boldly”.
عَمَّ يَتَسَاءَلُونَ is the opening of Sūrat al-Naba’, sūra 78, not 74 (al-Muddaththir).

find: with a son of mine, who said: 'So I was shown him, and I said when I saw him:
replace: with a son of mine, and I pointed him out to him, and I said when I saw him:
reason: وَمَعِي ابْنٌ لِي، قَالَ: فَأَرَيْتُهُ، فَقُلْتُ لَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُ: the قال is the narrator Abū Rimtha resuming, not his son speaking. The dataset vocalises فَأَرَيْتُهُ (“I showed him [to my son]”); other versions read فَأُرِيتُهُ (“I was shown him”), so the exact wording needs a scholar.

find: "Color the edges of the eyelids with antimony ,and three times in that.
reason: Truncated. The Arabic continues: فَإِنَّهُ يَجْلُو الْبَصَرَ، وَيُنْبِتُ الشَّعْرَ وَزَعَمَ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ كَانَتْ لَهُ مُكْحُلَةٌ يَكْتَحِلُ مِنْهَا كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ، ثَلاثَةً فِي هَذِهِ، وَثَلاثَةً فِي هَذِهِ. The English drops the benefits, the kohl-pot and the nightly use. Needs a full translation.

find: he would pause periodically, so that
replace: he would speak clearly and distinctly, so that
reason: يَتَكَلَّمُ بِكَلامٍ بَيِّنٍ فَصْلٍ: بَيِّن is “clear” and فَصْل “distinct / separated”. “Pause periodically” is one reading of فصل but drops بيّن.

find: anyone with a more cheerful countenance than
reason: أَكْثَرَ تَبَسُّمًا is literally “more smiling”. “A more cheerful countenance” is a paraphrase that loses تبسّم, which the chapter on his smiling contrasts with ضحك.

The English only says “Same as the above hadith”, but this Arabic differs from the one before it: it ends إِلا تَبَسَّمَ (“without smiling”) where the previous one has إِلا ضَحِكَ (“without laughing”), and the word order differs. The narrator (عَنْ جَرِيرٍ) is also blank. Needs its own translation.

find: He recited in a quivering voice.
replace: He recited with tarjī‘ (repeating and modulating his voice).
reason: فَقَرَأَ وَرَجَّعَ. The same verb رجّع is rendered “quivering voice” here and “quavering tone” in shamail:308 (لا يُرَجِّعُ). Neither is standard; tarjī‘ is the technical term. A scholar should pick one rendering for both.

find: he did not chant in a quavering tone.
replace: he did not use tarjī‘ (repeating and modulating his voice).
reason: وَكَانَ لا يُرَجِّعُ: same verb as فَقَرَأَ وَرَجَّعَ in shamail:307, which is rendered differently. The two reports look contradictory and commentators reconcile them, so the rendering should be decided with a scholar.

find: Our ears were open and we were listening to what he was saying, while we were in our dwellings.
replace: Our hearing was opened, so that we could hear what he was saying while we were in our dwellings.
reason: فَفُتِحَتْ أَسْمَاعُنَا حَتَّى كُنَّا نَسْمَعُ مَا يَقُولُ وَنَحْنُ فِي مَنَازِلِنَا: فُتِحَتْ is passive (“was opened”) and حَتَّى gives the result (“so that we could hear”). The English loses that their hearing was opened for them.
